title: SRE: SLOs, Error Budgets, Capacity Planning, Reliability Initiatives, Incident Review Standards, Operational Tooling, and Runbooks
author: Ari Chen
content:
Overview

This document defines Redwood Inference SRE standards for service-level objectives (SLOs) and error budgets, capacity planning, reliability initiatives, incident review standards, operational tooling, and canonical runbooks. It is intended as the single-source guidance for teams operating production inference services (hosted, dedicated, and private).

Goals
- Establish measurable SLOs and a clear error budget policy that balances developer velocity and customer reliability.
- Provide repeatable capacity planning and scaling practices to meet latency and throughput targets.
- Standardize incident review and postmortem hygiene to drive prevention work.
- Define the operational tooling baseline and canonical runbooks for common failure modes.

1) SLOs and Error Budgets

Intro and scope
- SLOs in scope: public inference API (generation/chat/embeddings), control plane (job submission, model rollouts), and internal platform services (scheduler, routing, KV-cache).
- Measurement: all SLOs are measured at the service ingress (edge/proxy) for customer-visible requests. Internal SLOs measured at service-to-service RPC boundaries where appropriate.

Primary SLOs (examples and targets)
- Inference API (production): availability = 99.95% (30d rolling window); latency p95 <= 250ms for prompt length <= 128 tokens, p99 <= 800ms.
- Control plane (model rollouts / config APIs): availability = 99.9% (30d).
- Dedicated capacity scheduler: scheduling success rate >= 99.5% and queue time p95 < 2s.
- KV cache hit rate objective: >= 85% for frequently used prefixes (depends on model workload).

Error budget windows and rules
- Window: 30-day rolling window; 7-day short window used for rapid triage.
- Error budget = (1 - SLO) * window duration (e.g., for 99.95% availability, 0.05% of 30 days ≈ 21.6 minutes).
- Burn thresholds and actions (per-service):
  1. Advisory: 0–10% burn — notify service owner and SRE lead; create a monitoring ticket.
  2. Mitigation plan required: 10–30% burn — schedule a mitigation/stopgap within 24 hours; escalate to platform SRE if cross-service.
  3. Deploy freeze + remediation: 30–60% burn — halt non-critical deploys; require rollback or canary reduction; run focused investigation and apply mitigations within 48 hours.
  4. Emergency response: > 60% burn — engage incident response war room, prioritize customer-impacting remediation; executive notif.
- Burn rate alerts: configured for 1h/6h/24h burn rate; alert targets include service owner, on-call SRE, and engineering manager.

SLO ownership and reporting
- Each service must declare: SLO owner (on-call engineer), SLO steward (team lead), and a 1–2 sentence definition of customer impact.
- Monthly SLO review in SRE guild: compare SLO performance, identify recurring error budget classes, and prioritize reliability initiatives.

2) Capacity Planning

Principles
- Design for predictable tail latency and steady throughput rather than best-case throughput.
- Maintain operational headroom: target reserve = 40% of steady-state capacity to absorb spikes and maintenance.
- Capacity should be planned per-tier (hosted API, dedicated pools, private deployments).

Key inputs and formulas
- Inputs: request RPS distribution (p50/p95/p99), average tokens generated per request, model type and per-GPU throughput profile, KV cache hit rate, batching efficiency, and SLA latency targets.
- Baseline capacity formula (simplified): Required GPUs = ceil( (peak_RPS * avg_tokens_per_request) / (tokens_per_second_per_gpu * effective_batch_factor * (1 - reserve)) )
  - tokens_per_second_per_gpu: measured in benchmark runs for model + quantization profile.
  - effective_batch_factor: accounts for batching and batching latency tradeoff (e.g., 1.0–3.0 depending on workload).

Autoscaling and thresholds
- Horizontal scaling preferred for stateless frontends; vertical for capacity-heavy model pools when pinned to limited GPU types.
- Scale-up triggers (one or more): sustained p95 latency > SLO for 10m AND GPU utilization > 70% OR queue length > 5 for 5m.
- Scale-down: sustained utilization < 40% for 20m AND p95 latency comfortably below SLO.
- Canary warm-up: new instances must complete a warm-up probe (KV cache prefill, model cold-start verification) before being routed production traffic.

Planning cadence and forecasting
- Quarterly capacity review: project growth, committed capacity for Dedicated customers, and major model onboarding impacts.
- Monthly delta review: review headroom, bursting events, and adjust autoscaling policies if needed.

3) Reliability Initiatives (RIs)

RI lifecycle
1. Identification: SRE or product team proposes an RI tied to error budget history, incident trends, or business priorities. Provide hypothesis and expected ROI (reduced MTTR, lower error budget burn, cost impact).
2. Triage & prioritization: evaluate impact, cost to fix, and implementation risk. Prioritize using RICE-style scoring and align with product roadmap.
3. Implementation: tracked in a project ticket with milestones, owners, test plan, and rollout strategy (canary, A/B).
4. Validation: post-rollout metrics and guardrail checks; measure change in SLO performance and cost.
5. Close & retro: document results in the RI ticket and add learnings to SRE knowledge base.

Example RIs
- Improve prefix/KV cache invalidation strategy to increase cache hit rate from 70% to 85% for common workloads — estimated 18% per-token cost savings.
- Kernel selection automation to reduce tail latency for long-context prompts — estimated p99 latency reduction of 40–60ms.

4) Incident Review Standards (Postmortems)

Mandatory postmortems
- Any SEV2/SEV1 incident impacting customers or any incident that exhausts >30% error budget requires a postmortem.

Postmortem template (required fields)
- Title (short)
- Incident start/end times (UTC)
- Severity classification and customer impact summary
- Timeline of events (annotated, minute-level where possible)
- Root cause analysis (RCA) and contributing factors
- Mitigations applied during incident and why they were chosen
- Long-term fixes (action items with owners and due dates)
- Error budget impact and metrics
- Follow-up verification plan and success criteria
- Distribution list (who was notified)

Review process and SLAs
- Postmortem draft due within 72 hours of incident containment.
- Review meeting scheduled within 7 days; reviewers include SRE on-call, service owner, product manager, and a cross-team reviewer.
- Action items must have clear owners and due dates; tracked in the reliability initiatives backlog.

5) Operational Tooling (minimum baseline)

Monitoring and alerting
- Metrics: requests/sec, error rate (4xx/5xx), latency p50/p95/p99, GPU utilization, queue length, cache hit rate, batch size distribution.
- Logs: structured JSON request traces with correlation IDs (trace_id, request_id, user_tenant_id where allowed).
- Traces: distributed traces with span-level durations for model inference, KV cache lookup, scheduling, and network egress.
- Alerting: use tiered alerting (info/warning/critical) mapped to runbooks and on-call rotations.

Runbook and playbook platform
- Single-source runbooks stored in Confluence with links from alert pages in paging system. Runbooks must include required RBAC roles, CLI commands, dashboard links, and rollback steps.

Tooling list (recommended)
- Metrics: Prometheus + Thanos / Cortex for long retention, Grafana for dashboards.
- Tracing: OpenTelemetry -> Jaeger/Tempo.
- Logging: ELK/Opensearch or managed SaaS depending on customer confidentiality.
- Paging: PagerDuty or equivalent for on-call alerting.
- ChatOps: Slack with incident channels and an incident bot for status updates.
- Chaos/Load: internal load-generator harness used for capacity validation and game days.

6) Canonical SRE Runbooks (examples)

Runbook: High p95/p99 Inference Latency (production inference API)
- Symptoms:
  - p95 latency > SLO for > 10 minutes and trend rising.
  - Increased queue length at inference frontends; GPU utilization > 75%.
- Immediate actions (first 15 minutes):
  1. Acknowledge alert and create incident channel.
  2. Identify scope: run query on metrics dashboard (service, region, model_id, route).
     - Grafana query examples: 
       - requests/sec by model: sum(rate(inference_requests_total{job=~"inference.*"}[1m])) by (model_id)
       - latency p95: histogram_quantile(0.95, sum(rate(inference_request_duration_seconds_bucket[5m])) by (le, model_id))
  3. If the issue is isolated to a model variant, shift traffic to a healthy variant or fallback model (use routing console to modify route weight).
  4. If queues indicate backpressure, temporarily increase worker pool size (if autoscaling cannot catch up): 
     - kubectl scale deployment inference-worker --replicas=<new-count> -n inference-prod
  5. If caches are cold (large spike after deploy), initiate cache prefill using warm-up job: 
     - /opt/internal/bin/cache-prefill --model model_id --targets=50
- Remediation & follow-ups (30–120 minutes):
  - If mitigation holds, monitor error budget burn and schedule a deeper RCA.
  - If mitigation fails, start rollback of the offending deploy or reduce canary percentage to 0.
  - Collect profiler traces from a representative request and upload to shared bucket for runtime team.

Runbook: Service Unavailable / 5xx Spike
- Symptoms: sustained 5xx rate > 0.5% of traffic for > 5 minutes.
- Steps:
  1. Triage: determine whether error class is client-side (4xx) or server-side (5xx).
  2. Check recent deploys: review deployment timeline and canary events.
  3. Revert last deploy if correlated with spike and if revert is low-risk.
  4. If database / external dependency is failing, enable degraded mode (read-only, reduce feature flags) and inform product.
  5. Notify customers via status page if impact is widespread.

Runbook: Capacity Exhaustion / GPU OOMs
- Symptoms: GPU OOM events, scheduler rejection, or crash loops after model onboarding.
- Steps:
  1. Isolate offending model / version and take it out of rotation.
  2. Check model memory profile and quantization profile; try a lower-memory variant (int8 or bf16) if available.
  3. If memory leak suspected, collect heap/dump and open ticket with runtime team.
  4. Apply capacity increase (if safe) and rerun validation traffic in canary.

Ownership, escalation, and SLAs
- On-call: every service must have at least one primary and one secondary on-call engineer; SRE team provides cross-service escalation.
- Escalation path: on-call -> SRE lead -> engineering manager -> VP Eng for Sev1.
- SLAs for response: Critical (pager) must be acknowledged within 5 minutes; action started within 15 minutes.

Appendix: Metrics, Dashboards & Templates
- Required dashboards: service overview, latency heatmap by model and region, error budget burn rate, capacity utilization heatmap, deployment timeline.
- Standard Grafana dashboard IDs: add links to team dashboards and include sample queries in runbooks.
- Postmortem template: store canonical template at /confluence/eng-sre/postmortem-template.

Operational hygiene checklist (weekly)
- Verify alert-to-runbook links for top 20 alerts.
- Review error budget burn for all services and assign actions for any >10% burn.
- Run a smoke test for model cold-starts and KV cache warm-up.

Conformance and audits
- Quarterly audit: SRE leadership verifies that every production service has declared SLOs, owners, runbooks, and an assigned on-call.
- Compliance evidence: for Private deployments, capture SLO configurations and audit logs per customer as part of compliance packages.
